findings.explanation: The PR removed the ownership scoping filter from the GET /orders/mine handler. Base code filtered with `.filter(Order.user_id == g.current_user.id)` (app/routes/orders.py:43); the PR replaces it with `.filter(Order.status != "cancelled")` (app/routes/orders.py:43), so the query now returns every non-cancelled order in the database regardless of the requester. The only remaining check is `@require_auth` (app/auth.py:55-66), which authenticates the caller and sets g.current_user but performs no ownership verification. This violates security-policy.md §3 ('A user may view ONLY their own orders') and api-spec.md ('/orders/mine | GET | any authenticated user (own orders only)'). Because Order.to_dict() exposes user_id, total, and shipping_address (app/models.py:55-62), any authenticated user can now read other users' order data — a classic IDOR / broken object-level authorization.

evidence.content:
## 3. Order data access rules
- A user may view ONLY their own orders. Every endpoint that fetches an order by its identifier MUST verify ownership with `is_owner_or_admin(current_user, order.user_id)` before returning data.
- Listing another user's orders is restricted to that user themselves and administrators.
| `/orders/mine` | GET | any authenticated user (own orders only) |

findings.suggested_fix: Restore the ownership scoping so the query only returns the requester's orders, e.g. `.filter(Order.user_id == g.current_user.id, Order.status != "cancelled")`. If admins should be able to list all orders here, gate that with `is_owner_or_admin`/role logic, but the default path must remain scoped to the authenticated user's own orders.
